header_parsing.justification: The recommendation matches what I implemented: header=[0, 1] for tracks.csv and header=[0, 1, 2] for features.csv, with index_col=0 so track_id becomes the index and the header rows are not read as data. I also used its alternative, flattening the MultiIndex to names like mfcc_mean_01 right after loading, because scikit-learn and parquet need flat string column names. Its warning about misaligned track_ids is valid; I handle it by selecting features through the index intersection with the fma_small track IDs and joining Echonest data on track_id, never by row order.

missing_genre.justification: I accepted the core advice: tracks without genre_top cannot be used to train or evaluate a supervised classifier, and the mostly empty metadata columns (77.95% to 99.71% missing) are not carried forward. I modified one part: I do not delete the 56,976 unlabeled tracks from the dataset. They stay in the general EDA (duration, listens, release years) and are excluded only from genre-based tests and models. I rejected the semi-supervised alternative: the pseudo-labels would be produced by the same audio features I am evaluating, which is circular, and in FMA a missing genre_top means the track has several top-level genres or none, so forcing one label onto it would be wrong by design. Its selection-bias warning is fair: my genre results describe tracks with a single top-level genre only.

duration_outliers.justification: I agreed with the main point: the 16 zero-length tracks are impossible values, and the 7,010 tracks outside the log-IQR fences [50.6 s, 900.6 s] should not be dropped, because duration is not a model input and long DJ mixes or live sets are real recordings. I modified the treatment of the zero-length tracks: instead of deleting the rows, I set their duration to missing, because their other fields (genre, listens, dates) are still valid for EDA. The IQR result is kept as a flag column and reported in Figure 3, not used as a filter. I rejected its alternative of removing all 7,010 flagged tracks (about 6.6% of the data), since there is no evidence that their audio features were extracted incorrectly.

listens_skew.justification: Accepted for EDA: log1p reduces skewness from 24.5 to 0.09 and handles the one zero-listen track, so listens are analyzed and plotted on the log1p scale. For the correlation test I used its alternative, Spearman's rank correlation, and corrected its reasoning. Spearman works on ranks, and log1p does not change the order of the values, so rho is identical on raw and log-transformed listens. The real choice is Pearson on log1p versus Spearman. I chose Spearman because it does not assume a linear relationship and is robust to the remaining heavy tail. Its point that the 13,129 Echonest tracks may not represent the full dataset is valid and is listed as a limitation.

model_choice.justification: The recommendation matches my design: L2-regularized Logistic Regression as the baseline (C = 0.01 chosen on validation), gradient-boosted trees as the advanced model, macro-F1 plus a confusion matrix as the metrics, and no SMOTE, because fma_small has exactly 1,000 tracks per genre. I added Random Forest as a second advanced model and k-NN as a reference from my proposal. I did not follow its suggestion to add cross-validation on the training set: the official FMA split keeps each artist in only one split, while random CV folds would put the same artist in training and validation and inflate scores. Keeping the official split also makes my results comparable with other work on FMA. I rejected the SVC-on-family-aggregates alternative because averaging features within a family throws away information, with no clear benefit at this data size.

prompt_comparison.justification: The naive prompt produced a generic tutorial: three methods with Python and Excel code. Its top recommendation, keeping only tracks between 30 seconds and 10 minutes, would have deleted every track over 10 minutes, including all 139 tracks over an hour, and it never asked whether duration matters for the model. The structured prompt used the actual numbers (16 zero-length tracks, 139 over an hour, 7,010 outside the log-IQR fences), noticed that duration is not a classifier input, and recommended removing only the impossible values, which is what the data supports. I rejected the naive answer's advice and based the decision on the structured response. The difference came from giving the model the project goal, a data summary and a required answer format.

interpret_results.justification: I checked every number against the context and all of them match (Gradient Boosting macro-F1 0.490 vs. chance 0.125, top-2 accuracy 0.681, Folk F1 0.19, MFCC importance 0.200), so there is no hallucination. Its central finding agrees with my conclusions: Folk is the weakest genre and sits at the centre of the confusions. Instrumental (26%) and International (23%) tracks are often predicted as Folk, and Folk tracks are spread across Pop, Experimental and International. I modified the explanation: 'acoustically similar genres' and 'shared instrumentation' are plausible but untested, so the report presents them as one possible explanation alongside overlapping genre labels. I did not follow the advice to 're-examine Folk boundaries', because the labels come from the dataset and changing them would change the ground truth. I did not adopt the hierarchical-classification alternative, which goes beyond this project's research question.

test_choice.justification: I checked the response against the context: Levene p = 1.36e-137, Welch F(10, 827.6) = 1119.65, and N = 9,338 (the group counts add up to this) all match. It also exposed two problems in my original analysis. My rule switched to Kruskal-Wallis whenever residuals were non-normal, even though my H0 is about mean energy, and Kruskal-Wallis compares rank distributions, not means. My post-hoc test was Tukey HSD, which assumes equal variances, the exact assumption Levene rejects here. Its argument for Welch holds: the smallest group (Blues) still has 66 tracks, so the group means are approximately normal by the central limit theorem even though the residuals are not. I therefore accepted the recommendation and changed the code: Welch's ANOVA is now the primary test, Games-Howell replaces Tukey (I checked my implementation against the pingouin library), and I report omega-squared next to eta-squared. I kept its alternative, Kruskal-Wallis with Holm-corrected pairwise tests, as a robustness check, because of the skewness risk it pointed out (Classical: mean 0.071 vs. median 0.044). All three tests agree (p < 0.001).
